content: 1. Temperature and Warmth Assessment: It is important to assess the newborn's body temperature by feeling for warmth. A temperature of 4°C indicates mild hypothermia, requiring immediate rewarming through skin-to-skin contact with the mother. If the temperature does not improve after two hours, reassess the baby. 2. Mother Unable to Breastfeed: If the mother is unable to breastfeed due to receiving special treatment or other reasons, assist her in expressing breast milk. Consider alternative feeding methods until the mother recovers. 3. Normal Weight and Feeding: A baby weighing 2500 grams or more, feeding effectively at least eight times in 24 hours, and showing no danger signs or special treatment needs is classified as a well baby. Before discharge, immunize the baby if due, advise on routine postnatal visits, and educate the mother on when to return if danger signs appear. 4. Preterm or Low Birth Weight Babies: Babies born preterm (less than 37 weeks) or with a birth weight under 2500 grams require special attention. If the baby weighs less than 1500 grams, urgent referral to a hospital is necessary, ensuring extra warmth during transport. For babies weighing 1500–2500 grams, provide kangaroo mother care (continuous skin-to-skin contact), support breastfeeding, and monitor daily. Do not discharge until the baby is feeding well, gaining weight, and maintaining a stable body temperature. 5. Twins: Mothers of twins require additional support to breastfeed both babies effectively. Discharge should only occur when both twins are ready to go home. 6. Breastfeeding Assessment: Evaluate breastfeeding in every baby as part of routine examinations. If the baby is not feeding adequately or has not breastfed within six hours of birth, urgent referral to a hospital is required. 7. Feeding Difficulties: If the baby is breastfeeding less than eight times in 24 hours, receiving other foods or drinks, or not feeding adequately, provide support for exclusive breastfeeding. Reassess at the next feed or follow-up visit in two days. 8. Special Treatment Needs: Check the mother’s medical history for conditions such as fever, prolonged membrane rupture, or infections like syphilis or HIV. If the baby is at risk of bacterial infection, administer antibiotics for five days and assess daily. For HIV-exposed infants, administer antiretroviral therapy and counsel the mother on safe feeding options. 9. Jaundice and Local Infections: Examine the baby for signs of jaundice, particularly yellowing of the skin or eyes. Severe jaundice in babies less than 24 hours old requires urgent hospital referral. For local infections such as umbilical redness or skin pustules, teach the mother appropriate treatment and follow up in two days. If no improvement is seen, refer the baby to a hospital. 10. Danger Signs: Monitor for danger signs such as fast or slow breathing, severe chest in-drawing, poor feeding, grunting, convulsions, or abnormal movements. If any of these signs are present, administer the first dose of antibiotics and urgently refer the baby to a hospital. 11. Birth Injuries and Malformations: Handle the baby gently and avoid forcing limbs into unnatural positions. For severe malformations, refer the baby for specialized treatment and plan for follow-up care. 12. Breast Health in Mothers: Teach correct breastfeeding techniques and encourage continued breastfeeding. For mastitis, provide antibiotics and reassess in two days. If no improvement occurs, refer the mother to a hospital. 13. General Newborn Care: Keep the baby close to the mother, dressed warmly, and covered with a blanket. Support exclusive breastfeeding on demand and teach the mother proper baby care, including hygiene and cord care. Do not expose the baby to direct sunlight or place them on cold surfaces. 14. Small Baby or Twin Care: For small babies (weighing 1500–2500 grams) or twins, plan for a longer hospital stay before discharge. Provide additional warmth, encourage frequent breastfeeding, and assess feeding daily. If feeding difficulties persist for three days or weight loss exceeds 10% of birth weight, refer for breastfeeding counseling. 15. Replacement Feeding: If the mother chooses replacement feeding, assess the baby’s feeding practices and teach proper cup feeding techniques. Reassess at the next feed or follow-up visit. 16. Routine Examinations: Examine all newborns routinely around an hour after birth, before discharge, and during postnatal visits in the first week of life. Record findings in the postnatal and home-based records. Always conduct examinations in the presence of the mother.
